title: Security Onion Timeline Analysis
subtitle: Simulated Windows compromise · network evidence, host activity and incident chronology
description: An individual Security Onion midterm investigation of a simulated Windows compromise. The recovered submitted report and timeline diagram document the student's analysis of executable retrieval, command-and-control, host reconnaissance and possible outbound archive transfer.
problem: Explain a simulated attack sequence using multiple evidence sources.
approach: Correlated Suricata alert records, HTTP transaction metadata and network flow observations into an incident timeline. Documented suspicious execution, command-and-control and system enumeration, evaluated an outbound archive signature, mapped findings to ATT&CK techniques and recommended containment.
outcome: Midterm graded 86.25/100. Instructor praised the diagram and corrected the initial infection sequence: a user downloaded a malicious executable, which then launched PowerShell to retrieve additional files. Hashes, VirusTotal scores and Sysmon command evidence were missing. The report's stronger conclusions are analyst interpretations, not independently verified results.
impact: Graded incident timeline and written investigation with documented evidence limitations.
evidenceNote: Reopened Canvas submission: original report, timeline PDF and two screenshot attachments recovered; three other listed screenshots still absent. The screenshot shown is a redacted crop. Instructor corrections and missing host/hash evidence are explicitly preserved.

evidenceImages.caption: Original submitted Security Onion SOC 1 screenshot, cropped and redacted: executable-download rule details. This is midterm evidence, not the separate final report.

architecture: Simulated initial executable download → Windows endpoint
Follow-on PowerShell activity → Additional file retrieval
Suricata alerts and HTTP records → Network event correlation
Reported command-and-control and enumeration → Analyst chronology
Outbound archive indicator → Investigative assessment (not independently rerun)
Incident report and timeline → Recommended containment and documented gaps

title: AWS VPC Peering
subtitle: Blue Bear VPC peering · bidirectional private database connectivity and route recovery
description: An individual AWS architecture studio exercise connecting two separate store VPCs. The October 23 evidence packet documents active peering, bidirectional TLS-verified database queries, least-privilege access and a controlled routing failure with successful recovery.
problem: Design peering and bidirectional routes with scoped access.
approach: Configured Store 01 peering, added partner routes to public and private route tables, scoped database access to the partner EC2 host, set up read-only access, and coordinated reciprocal testing. Removed only the peer route to isolate the failure, confirmed local access still worked, restored the route, and retested.
outcome: The evidence packet documents six readable rows in each direction with TLS verified, peer-only failure after route removal and successful recovery. VPC peering activity graded 28/28; network diagram artifact 24/24. Earlier architecture archive indicated peering pending; the later October 23 packet documents the subsequent successful test. Not an ongoing production service.
impact: Documented two-way private database access, verified TLS and controlled routing failure recovery in a graded lab.
evidenceNote: October 23 evidence packet, page 7 screenshot and pages 6–11 test records support the successful lab result. Sensitive lab identifiers omitted; current availability not verified.

evidenceImages.caption: Actual Blue Bear application dashboard, cropped from the October 23 VPC evidence packet (p. 7). Two configured stores; peer RDS reachable; database TLS verified.

architecture: Store 01 EC2 application → Local private RDS with TLS
Store 01 routing tables → Active VPC peering connection
Peer VPC routing → Partner private RDS with restricted access

title: AWS High Availability & Resilience
subtitle: Two-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling and Application Load Balancer lab
description: An AWS Academy scalable and highly available Café challenge, accompanied by a Blue Bear architecture transfer analysis and a troubleshooting record. The recovered originals document a working lab application and the student's scaling configuration decisions, not measured disaster recovery.
problem: Select availability patterns and reason about failure and recovery.
approach: Configured a second-AZ NAT gateway, EC2 launch template, Auto Scaling group across two private subnets, and a public Application Load Balancer. The group used minimum two, desired two and maximum six instances. Investigated unhealthy target health checks and verified HTTP access and instance system checks. Identified a missing dynamic scaling policy in the grader, then documented configuring CPU target tracking at 25% with 60-second warmup.
outcome: Original AWS console screenshot shows two instances healthy at desired capacity across two Availability Zones. The submitted analysis reports a working café site through the ALB. Canvas records the challenge at 20/20 and failure-analysis artifact at 24/24. The troubleshooting record did not show a completed CPU stress test, measured failover or verified database HA.
impact: Documented scalable AWS lab architecture, health-check investigation and Auto Scaling policy troubleshooting.
evidenceNote: Recovered Auto Scaling screenshot, challenge result, individual transfer analysis and troubleshooting report. The assignment verifies lab deployment and reported website access; recovery objectives are targets, not observed failover measurements.
architecture: Public application request → Application Load Balancer
Load balancer → EC2 application instances in two private subnets
EC2 launch template → Auto Scaling group (min 2 / desired 2 / max 6)
Second-AZ NAT gateway → Outbound connectivity
Health checks and CPU utilization → Scaling configuration and troubleshooting
